Talmon
tal'mon
n. (a chief of the porters of the house of the LORD, whose family kept the gates from the days of David to the days of Nehemiah)
From Hebrew Talmon, of uncertain derivation, connected by some with telem, a furrow, and by others with a root meaning oppressed. The name attaches to a house rather than to a single life: the children of Talmon return in the register of the captivity centuries after the man.

Biblical Definition

Talmon is named among the porters — the gatekeepers of the sanctuary, an office the Chronicler treats with the seriousness of the priesthood itself. “And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief” (1Ch 9:17). The work was not ornamental. The porters lodged round about the house of God, opened it every morning, kept the chambers and the treasuries, counted the vessels in and out, and had charge of who came through the gate — because Scripture is emphatic that not everyone might come in, and no unclean thing was to enter. When the captivity ended, the list of those who came up includes the doorkeepers by household: “The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon” (Ezr 2:42). They are still there when the wall is finished: “Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two” (Neh 11:19), and again in Nehemiah's roll of the ministers, “were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates” (Neh 12:25). A family of doorkeepers, faithful across five hundred years and two temples, who never preached a sermon or sang a psalm and without whom the house would have stood open to anything.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Talmon; in sacred history he is a chief of the porters, or doorkeepers, of the house of the LORD.

expand to see more

TALMON, n. A proper name in the Hebrew Scriptures; a Levite of the order of the porters.

The porters kept the gates of the house of God and lodged round about it.

They had the oversight of the chambers, the treasuries and the holy vessels.

The children of Talmon returned from the captivity with Zerubbabel.

In the days of Nehemiah the porters that kept the gates were an hundred seventy and two.

Key Scripture

1Ch 9:17 — "And the porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon, and Ahiman, and their brethren: Shallum was the chief;"

Ezr 2:42 — "The children of the porters: the children of Shallum, the children of Ater, the children of Talmon, the children of Akkub, the children of Hatita, the children of Shobai, in all an hundred thirty and nine."

Neh 11:19 — "Moreover the porters, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two."

Neh 12:25 — "Mattaniah, and Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, Akkub, were porters keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that guarding the door of God's house is a ministry, that some things must be kept out, and that the man at the threshold is doing holy work.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Talmon is a doorkeeper in a list and nobody has contested him. What his office sets against the present church is the whole idea of a threshold. The porters existed because the house of the LORD had a boundary; there were courts the uncircumcised did not enter, vessels the unconsecrated did not touch, and days on which the gate stayed shut. To keep the ward was to say no at the right times, and the Chronicler counts the men who did it and writes down their names.

The principle to recover is the discipline of the visible church. Christ committed keys to His church (Mat 16:19; Mat 18:17-18), and the Supper is fenced: “he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself” (1Co 11:29). A congregation that has no porters — no membership, no examination, no elders willing to stand at the threshold — has not become more loving; it has abolished an office God appointed and left the treasuries unwatched. And the honour of the work is settled by the psalm: “I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness” (Psa 84:10).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Talmon (H2929), Talmon; sho'er (H7778), porter, gatekeeper; mishmereth (H4931), ward, charge, watch; saph (H5592), threshold, doorway; lishkah (H3957), chamber of the temple.

expand to see more

Hebrew Talmon (H2929) — Talmon; a chief of the porters and the head of a house.

Hebrew sho'er (H7778) — porter, gatekeeper; the Authorized Version's ‘porter’.

Hebrew mishmereth (H4931) — ward, watch, charge; what the porters kept.

Hebrew saph (H5592) — threshold; the place of their standing.

Hebrew lishkah (H3957) — chamber; the temple rooms in their keeping.

Usage

"“The porters were, Shallum, and Akkub, and Talmon” — doorkeepers written into the sacred register."

"“The children of Talmon” — a house still at the gate after the captivity."

"“Keeping the ward at the thresholds of the gates” — the office described in full."
